items.prompt: What does 'capture' mean in this unit?
choices: Getting an idea out of your head fast, before it fades
Rewriting an idea in your own words, a few days later, at a desk
Linking a note to several related notes you already have stored
items.explanation: Capture is the fast first step. Rewriting and linking come later.

items.prompt: Which failure does the shoebox of receipts stand for?
choices: Filing so carefully that you stop saving
Saving everything while processing nothing
Tossing each one out
items.explanation: The shoebox keeps everything but gives no quick way back to it.

items.prompt: What tends to happen when every note needs perfect filing at the moment of capture?
choices: You find every note instantly, for years on end, with no effort at all
Notes get better
You quietly stop capturing because of the friction
items.explanation: Friction at the worst moment kills the habit.

items.prompt: How much does a good in-the-moment capture need to contain?
choices: A phrase is enough
A polished, complete essay on the topic
A full copy of the source material
items.explanation: The capture only has to be a cue. Polish comes later, if at all.

items.prompt: In the tax-day story, how long did finding one receipt take in the shoebox (an assumed number)?
choices: 2 min
25 min
120 min
items.explanation: 25 minutes for the shoebox against 2 for the cabinet.

items.prompt: In the cabinet, how many receipts sat in each folder?
items.explanation: 120 receipts across 12 folders is 10 each.

items.prompt: Which do working note systems favour?
choices: Quick, low-friction capture over perfect filing in the moment
Perfect filing over any quick capture
Reviewing old notes instead of capturing new ones
items.explanation: They sit between the two failures, leaning toward easy capture.

items.prompt: What is a saved note worth if you cannot get it back when needed?
choices: Full value, because it was saved
Almost nothing, since it cannot be used
Value that grows with the length of the note it sits in
items.explanation: A note matters only when it can be used.

items.prompt: One friend photographs every book page and files none of it. Another fills a seven-field form per note before reading on and has stopped reading new books. What are these two failures?
choices: The first too passive, the second too heavy
The first too heavy, the second too passive
Both too passive, differing only in format
Both too heavy, differing only in volume
items.explanation: Saving without processing is the shoebox. Over-structuring until you stop capturing is the over-built cabinet.
items.reference:
Two ways to fail
👟 Too passive: save everything, process nothing
🗄️ Too heavy: file so carefully you stop saving
✅ Survives: quick capture now, light filing later
Why: a note you cannot retrieve is worth little, and a system you stop using is worth nothing.
items.learnMore:
Capture fast, organise lightly

Working systems keep the in-the-moment step tiny, because friction there kills the habit. Filing and rewriting happen in a later, short pass.

Common mistake

Believing a more elaborate filing scheme at capture time is automatically a better system.
items.reflection: Think of a tool or habit you abandoned. Was it because it saved too little or because it asked too much at the wrong moment?

items.prompt: Required fields at capture go from 2 to 7 (assumed). What does this most plausibly change?
choices: How accurate every note you have already written is, in total
How likely you are to skip capturing when busy
How quickly you can find a note again after six months
How many links each of your existing notes still needs
items.explanation: Extra fields are friction paid at the busiest moment, so they mainly change whether capture happens.

Yes: a one-week delay makes it equal to the shoebox failure
No: filing later in one short pass is the pattern that lasts
No: any sitting under an hour is always acceptable, whatever else
items.explanation: The heavy failure is front-loaded friction at capture, not a short later pass.

choices: Keeping fewer items always beats keeping more of them
A bigger container always makes retrieval slower
Only the cabinet owner truly kept the receipts
Keeping something is not the same as being able to use it
items.explanation: Both kept everything. Only one could reach a given receipt quickly, which is what made it worth keeping.

items.prompt: What is 'processing' a raw capture?
choices: Copying it again into one much bigger shared document at night
Deleting it once the day is over
Rewriting it in your own words and saying why it mattered
items.explanation: Processing turns a fragment into your own thought.

items.prompt: Which of these is closest to a photocopy?
choices: An instructor's sentence pasted in unchanged
A restatement tied to a mistake of your own making
A short note about why the idea matters to you
items.explanation: Unchanged text has had no processing.

items.prompt: Compared with its source, an own-words note is often what?
choices: Longer and complete
Narrower, yet more useful to you
Identical in length
items.explanation: Priya's note dropped the 'studies show' framing and still won.

items.prompt: What should a processed note say besides the idea itself?
choices: Who else has read it
Which folder it lives in
Why it mattered to you
items.explanation: The reason it mattered is the handle that brings it back.

items.prompt: Reading Tom's pasted notes months later feels like what?
choices: Reading the source for the first time
Remembering your own thinking about the idea
Reviewing a short summary you once wrote
items.explanation: Without processing there is nothing of his own in them.

items.prompt: How many pasted pages did Tom end up with?
items.explanation: Forty-five pages, against Priya's six short notes.

items.prompt: When is the best time to process a capture?
choices: Never, memory copes
Only after a year
Soon after, ideally the same day
items.explanation: The sooner you process, the more context you still remember.

items.prompt: Which step turns a copy into something you understand?
choices: Processing
Capturing
Resurfacing
items.explanation: Capturing saves it and resurfacing meets it again, but only processing makes it yours.

items.prompt: Six months on, a pasted sentence sits beside a note saying 'I waited for the vendor to name a price and lost the framing'. Which is faster to use, and why?
choices: The second, because it already says why the idea mattered
The first, because it is the exact source wording the instructor chose
The first, because it is shorter and quicker to read in full
The second, because it contains more total facts than the first
items.explanation: Reuse speed depends on how much reconstruction is left to do. The second carries its own reason.
items.reference:
Same sentence, two notes
📄 Pasted: reads like new material later
🗒️ Rewritten: says why it mattered to you
↔️ The rewrite is often narrower, and still more useful
Why: restating an idea ties it to something you care about, which makes it fast to recall.
items.learnMore:
Processing makes a note yours

Rewriting forces you to decide what the idea actually means to you. That decision is what a copy never contains.

Common mistake

Judging a note by how much of the source it preserves instead of how quickly you can use it.
items.reflection: Pick one thing you learned recently. How would you restate it so that a friend with no background would see why it mattered to you?

items.prompt: Priya's note is narrower than the instructor's sentence. What follows?
choices: It is worse, because it dropped part of the source
It can still be more useful, tied to a real, specific call
It is equal, since both state one idea
It is worse, since it adds personal detail
items.explanation: Usefulness comes from retrievability and meaning, not completeness.

Changing the font size of the pasted sentence so it is clearer
Replacing it with a restatement plus the call it reminds you of

Nothing at all, since a fragment keeps its meaning for years
The ability to link it to any older note in the set
The context needed to rewrite it, so the rewrite gets harder

items.prompt: What is a link between two notes?
choices: A copy of one note placed inside of another note
A connection between notes on related ideas
A tag that records how old a given note is now
items.explanation: Links connect related ideas so that finding one surfaces the other.

items.prompt: What is resurfacing?
choices: Writing a note for the very first time
Deleting notes you no longer ever need to keep
Meeting an old note again at a useful moment
items.explanation: A note that never resurfaces gave no value.

items.prompt: How can an unlinked note usually be found?
choices: Only by remembering it exists and guessing the keyword
By following a trail from a neighbour
By luck while scrolling a list
items.explanation: With no links, search is the only door.

items.prompt: Which counts as resurfacing a note?
choices: Pasting the source into a new file
Following a link from a related note
Renaming the folder it lives in so it sorts first
items.explanation: A link trail is one of the valid ways back.

items.prompt: What is a 'second brain'?
choices: A backup copy of all of your earliest notes
A list of everything you have ever read
A note collection that helps you think
items.explanation: Notes that lead to each other help you reason.

items.prompt: Why do links help a forgotten note get found?
choices: They add routes from things you are already looking at
They make the note shorter and quicker to read
They make the note look neater and more complete in full
items.explanation: A need usually shows up next to something related.

items.prompt: Roughly how many related notes should one note link to?
choices: Every other note in the collection
A few, such as two or three
None, to keep it clean
items.explanation: A few cheap links are the sweet spot.

items.prompt: Is a formal weekly review the only way to resurface notes?
choices: Yes: nothing else counts
Yes, and daily
No: following a link or searching counts too
items.explanation: Any path back counts as resurfacing.

items.prompt: Two people own a note on the same idea. One linked theirs to three related notes, the other to none. Someone who has forgotten the idea exists is likelier to find which, and why?
choices: The linked one, because a neighbouring note leads to it
The unlinked one, because it has fewer routes to confuse you
Both equally, because the wording is identical
The unlinked one, because search handles everything
items.explanation: A forgotten idea cannot be searched by name, but a trail can reach it.
items.reference:
A note and its trails
🔗 Link: a connection to a related note
🧭 Trail: you land on a neighbour, then cross over
🔎 Search alone: needs a keyword you may have forgotten
Why: links give a forgotten note more than one way to be found.
items.learnMore:
Links are paths back

A note with no links can only be found by remembering it and guessing its keyword. Each link adds a route from something you are already looking at.

Common mistake

Linking every note to everything, which makes every route equally unhelpful.

items.prompt: A note is linked to about forty others. What is the most likely result?

Links stop carrying any signal
The note becomes much shorter and quicker to read
Nothing changes, since extra links are always free
items.explanation: When everything links to everything, a link carries no signal, so useful ones are harder to spot.

items.prompt: In which order do the loop's steps run?
choices: Capture, process, link, resurface
Link, capture, resurface, process
Resurface, capture, link, process
items.explanation: Capture gets the idea in. Processing and linking make it findable.

items.prompt: Which step has to happen in the moment?
choices: Process
Capture
Link
items.explanation: Only capture would be lost if delayed.

items.prompt: Why are the steps separated in time?
choices: Notes should always be left completely unread for a year
Linking is physically impossible while you are writing
Filing at capture time kills the habit
items.explanation: Separation keeps friction away from the busy moment.

items.prompt: Which pair of steps run together in the short later pass?
choices: Process and link
Capture and resurface
Resurface and capture
items.explanation: They ride along together, a few days after capture at most.

items.prompt: How long can a small unprocessed backlog reasonably exist?
choices: A whole year
A few days
Never
items.explanation: Brief backlogs are fine. Endless ones are not.

items.prompt: About how long does Priya's in-the-moment capture take?
choices: About 4 minutes
About 40 minutes
About 4 seconds
items.explanation: The capture is deliberately tiny.

items.prompt: What is an unprocessed capture worth if it is never revisited?
choices: About the same as no capture
More than a processed note
Exactly the worth of a link
items.explanation: It provides no value until someone processes it.

items.prompt: What does the 'reinforces' arrow in the loop mean?
choices: The note must be rewritten from scratch
Meeting a note again strengthens what you processed
It is deleted after one use
items.explanation: Resurfacing feeds back into the note.

items.prompt: Why does 'process' come before 'link' in the loop?
choices: You need the idea in your own words to see what it relates to
Links must exist before any idea is understood at all
Processing is simply the same step as capture
Linking is not allowed until a full week of review has been done
items.explanation: You can only connect an idea after you know what it says.
items.reference:
The loop, and when each step runs
⚡ Capture: seconds, in the moment
✍️ Process and 🔗 link: one short pass, later
🔎 Resurface: when a need or a link brings it back
Why: separating the steps in time keeps capture easy and still makes notes findable.
items.learnMore:
Decouple the steps

Capture has to be effortless to survive. Rewriting and linking can wait a short while, as long as the backlog does not grow forever.

Common mistake

Letting the backlog of unprocessed captures grow without limit.
items.reflection: Think of a routine you keep up. Which part of it do you do in the moment, and which part do you postpone to a calmer time?

Like no capture, because their context has faded
Better than the second person's, because there are more
Identical, because a fragment never loses its meaning
items.explanation: A fragment depends on memory, and memory fades faster than the backlog grows.

A fast fragment that is never revisited

Review it weekly
Capture it and let it go
items.explanation: Expiring logistics do not earn the processing pass.

items.prompt: Which notes earn the full processing pass?
choices: Ideas still worth caring about in six months
Anything that took under a minute to hear aloud
Every single fragment, with no exceptions at all
items.explanation: The pass is for what will be reused.

items.prompt: What stays non-negotiable under time pressure?
choices: Linking
Capture
A long rewrite
items.explanation: Capture costs seconds, so it always happens.

items.prompt: What may be deferred when the day has no spare time?
choices: The capture
Both the capture and the pass
The processing pass
items.explanation: Defer the pass, not the capture.

items.prompt: At 3 minutes of processing, the unit's assumed demo shows odds of about what?

items.prompt: Which fragment survives a one-week delay best?
choices: good point about pricing
anchor first even if rough - Kessler??
remember that thing
items.explanation: It carries a specific cue that points back to the exact moment.

items.prompt: In the assumed curve, where is the gain per minute largest?
choices: At the tenth minute
Evenly across every single minute
In the first few minutes
items.explanation: The curve rises steeply, then flattens.

items.prompt: Does the note 'deploy window moved to 3pm next Tuesday' need heavy processing?
choices: No: it expires within days
Yes: it needs two or three links to older notes
Yes: it should be rewritten in your own words first
items.explanation: Over-processing it repeats the over-organising failure.

items.prompt: Which of these deserves the full processing and linking pass?
choices: A rule of thumb that applies far beyond one deal
A reminder that Friday's meeting has moved to another room
A one-off discount code that expires this coming Sunday night
The number of a parking space for tomorrow morning only
items.explanation: Only the first will matter again in a new setting.
items.reference:
What gets the pass, what waits
✅ Ideas that will matter in six months: process and link
🗑️ Expiring logistics: capture and forget
⏳ No time tonight: keep the capture, defer the pass
Why: spend the processing minutes where they will be reused, and make fragments specific enough to survive a delay.

items.explanation: The fix costs a second or two at capture time: a name or a topic that points to the moment.
items.reference:
What gets the pass, what waits
✅ Ideas that will matter in six months: process and link
🗑️ Expiring logistics: capture and forget
⏳ No time tonight: keep the capture, defer the pass
Why: spend the processing minutes where they will be reused, and make fragments specific enough to survive a delay.
items.learnMore:
Triage and context

The first few minutes of processing carry most of the gain in the unit's assumed curve. A fragment with a specific cue can wait days. A vague one cannot.

Common mistake

Skipping the cue at capture time and hoping memory will fill the gap.
items.reflection: Think of a stream of information you face, such as a busy chat or a long reading list. How would you decide what earns a processing pass?
